source: CK-12 Physical Science Concepts for Middle School, CC-BY-NC
notes: Lesson on light bending at media boundaries. Structure: hook (straw-in-glass illusion) → definition of refraction → Snell's Law → index of refraction → diagram → examples (prism, lens) → video → practice.

units.label: Hook: straw in glass of water (image)
units.content_summary: Photograph of a straw in a glass of water appearing bent/broken at the water surface. Caption: 'Why does the straw appear to bend?'

units.label: Hook explanation (text)
units.content_summary: Explains that the straw appears bent because light changes speed when it moves from water to air, causing it to bend — this is refraction. Sets up the concept to be explored.

units.label: Learning Objectives (text)
units.content_summary: Objectives: define refraction; state Snell's Law; calculate index of refraction; explain how lenses and prisms use refraction; give real-world examples.

units.label: Definition: refraction (text)
units.content_summary: Refraction is the bending of light as it passes from one medium to another due to a change in speed. Light travels fastest in a vacuum (3×10⁸ m/s) and slower in denser media (glass, water). The change in speed causes the direction of light to change.

units.label: Refraction diagram: light ray bending (image)
units.content_summary: Diagram showing a light ray traveling from air into glass. Shows incident ray, normal line, refracted ray, angle of incidence (θ₁) and angle of refraction (θ₂). Ray bends toward normal when entering denser medium.

units.label: Index of refraction definition (text)
units.content_summary: Index of refraction n = c/v, where c is speed of light in vacuum and v is speed in the medium. Higher n = denser medium = more bending. Table of n values: vacuum=1.0, air≈1.0, water=1.33, glass=1.5, diamond=2.42.

units.label: Index of refraction table (image)
units.content_summary: Data table listing substances and their index of refraction values: vacuum(1.00), air(1.0003), water(1.33), glass(1.50), diamond(2.42). Sorted by increasing n value.

units.label: Snell's Law statement (text)
units.content_summary: Snell's Law: n₁ sin(θ₁) = n₂ sin(θ₂). Relates the angles of incidence and refraction to the indices of refraction of the two media. When going from less dense to more dense: ray bends toward normal. Reverse: bends away.

units.label: Worked Example: Snell's Law calculation (text)
units.content_summary: Problem: light travels from air (n=1.0) into glass (n=1.5) with angle of incidence 30°. Find angle of refraction. Solution: 1.0 × sin(30°) = 1.5 × sin(θ₂); sin(θ₂) = 0.5/1.5 = 0.333; θ₂ = 19.5°. Ray bends toward normal.

units.label: Application: prism and white light (text)
units.content_summary: A glass prism separates white light into a spectrum (rainbow of colours) because different wavelengths refract at slightly different angles. Violet refracts most, red least. Newton's prism experiment (1666).

units.label: Prism dispersion diagram (image)
units.content_summary: Diagram of white light entering a triangular prism and emerging as a spectrum (red, orange, yellow, green, blue, violet). Angles of refraction shown for red and violet. Classic dispersion illustration.

units.label: Application: converging and diverging lenses (text)
units.content_summary: Lenses use refraction to focus or diverge light. Converging (convex) lens: bends rays toward focal point — used in magnifying glasses, cameras, eyes. Diverging (concave) lens: spreads rays — used to correct nearsightedness.

units.label: Lens diagrams (image)
units.content_summary: Two diagrams: (1) converging lens with parallel rays bending to focal point F; (2) diverging lens with parallel rays bending outward, appearing to come from focal point F on same side as incoming light.

units.label: Video: refraction demonstrations (video)
units.content_summary: Video showing three refraction demonstrations: (1) laser in water tank bending; (2) coin disappearing/reappearing in water; (3) pencil-in-water trick explained with slow-motion ray tracing.

units.label: Practice problems (text)
units.content_summary: Four problems: (1) calculate angle of refraction using Snell's Law; (2) identify medium from n value; (3) determine type of lens for correcting vision; (4) explain why a swimming pool appears shallower than it is.
